$comment: The public API both SDKs must expose, and the places they deliberately differ.
The conformance suite tests SHARED behavior across four implementations, so a
capability that exists on one side only has no counterpart to disagree with and
the suite stays green by construction. Feature drift is invisible to a suite
shaped that way — which is how 0.9.0 shipped four Node-only additions, one of
which (`schema`) could silently split a deployment's queue in two.
Members are named in snake_case here; the TypeScript gate converts its own
camelCase names before comparing. Each SDK's gate asserts BOTH directions:
everything declared here exists there, AND everything there is declared here.
The second direction is the load-bearing one — it makes a one-sided addition
fail on the side that added it, at the moment it is added, rather than
surfacing as a missing feature on the other side a release later.
`internal` lists members that are not public API. TypeScript's `private` is
erased at runtime, so the Node gate cannot tell them apart on its own; Python's
leading underscore is checked by convention instead and needs no entry. Having
to add a name here when introducing a private method is the point: it asks
which kind of member it is while that is still a live question.
`only_node` / `only_py` are the deliberate asymmetries. Each carries a reason.
An entry here is a claim that the difference is idiomatic rather than a gap —
if it is a gap, the fix is to close it, not to list it.
`classes` gates the members of the three classes a caller drives. `modules` gates
what each SDK EXPORTS at all — the types, factories, predicates and errors reachable
from `import { … } from "cairnq"` / `from cairnq import …`. The two gates cover
different drift: 0.9.0's four Node-only additions were class members, but the same
mistake one level up (a helper, an error, an options type shipped on one side only)
was invisible until this section existed.
In `modules`, an exemption groups the members ONE reason covers (`members`,
plural) rather than repeating that reason per member. `classes` keeps the
singular `member` because each of its exemptions is argued on its own. Both
gates read either shape.
TypeScript names are canonicalized before comparing: a name starting with a capital
is a type or class and is already identical in both languages, anything else is
camelCase converted to snake_case. Python's declared surface is its `__all__`.

only_py.reason: Python's task() is a decorator, so registering a handler imperatively needs a second entry point. TypeScript's task() is already the imperative form and carries the same options as overloads.

only_node.reason: The lease-lost handle, in each language's own currency: an AbortSignal to hand to fetch here, an asyncio.Event to await there (cairnq-py's lease_lost). Same capability, and neither type exists in the other runtime.

only_py.reason: See TaskContext.signal under only_node — the same handle, as an asyncio.Event.

only_node.reason: TypeScript needs a named type for the options object a call takes; Python passes keyword arguments and needs no name for them. Same parameters, each declared where its language declares parameters.
A handler's signature is a named type in TypeScript and structural in Python, which types it inline on task() / register(). Nothing is exported because nothing needs a name.
The shape ctx.fail() accepts, as a named type. Python types the same argument inline on the method and exports nothing.
The row shape an executor hands back. Python's PgSession protocol types it inline as dict[str, Any], so there is no separate name to export.
A statically narrowed status type. Python has no static narrowing to export; the same constraint is enforced at runtime by validate_purge_input, and is_terminal_status answers it for a value.
Python's TaskDef is a dataclass, so TaskDef("name") constructs one directly. TypeScript's is an interface carrying phantom type parameters, which need a function call for the compiler to infer them.
